craft:Do this one.brief: NEW #craft card (the old guide had no craft section). Research NOW (WebSearch, ~5 calls): the best craft of the Saint-Tropez peninsula and the Maures a visitor can actually learn hands-on, with a named still-practising master and OPEN enrolment. Candidates: Cogolin — briar pipes (Courrieu, since 1802: visits?), the Manufacture des Tapis de Cogolin (hand-tufted carpets; visits?), Cogolin reeds for saxophone/clarinet (Rigotti; visits?); Saint-Tropez handmade sandals (Rondini since 1927, K.Jacques: made to measure, not taught); Collobrières/Maures cork; a pottery in the gulf that takes students. Pick the ONE that best meets: an unbroken local craft + named master + you can enrol. Rename the card (name = the place). Labels What you do · Time · Cost · Book. If nothing qualifies, make this card the honest best option and say what it lacks.

old.label: Bormes-les-Mimosas (La Favière
old.hook: A proper specialty coffee room down by the harbour: beans roasted locally, pulled on a La Marzocco, and a homemade all-day brunch. The kind of place that treats the espresso as the point rather than an afterthought to the rosé.

old.name: Soeurs Coffee & Bakery
old.label: Cavalaire-sur-Mer (in town)
old.hook: The honest truth: Cavalaire itself has no serious roaster, and Soeurs is the best in-town option — a coffee-shop-bakery-brunch run by Matthieu and Valentin, good for a flat white with a viennoiserie rather than a hunt for terroir beans. Treat it as convenience, not pilgrimage.

old.name: Côtes de Provence Rosé — the pale, bone-dry archetype
old.hook: The colour is a decision, not a dilution: these rosés are direct-pressed or briefly macerated, so the pink stays onion-skin pale while the wine drinks bone-dry and saline — the vines sit close enough to the sea to taste it. It is not the sweet blush the tint suggests. One thing to carry: buy the youngest vintage on the shelf and drink it cold this summer, not next.

old_also.name: Rosé de Provence (Côtes de Provence & Bandol)
old_also.text: The true drink of this coast and the honest local product. Côtes de Provence is the region's giant AOC, and rosé is roughly 80 percent of what Provence makes — the pale, near-salmon style from short skin contact and cold fermentation. Just west, tiny Bandol (about 1,600 ha) makes a darker, structured, age-worthy rosé and red built on Mourvèdre. Drink it cold, young, and cheaper than the sea view suggests. Origin Var / Provence; Côtes de Provence and Bandol (Bandol AOC created 1941), vines here since Roman times

old.name: Cru Classé Rosé — Provence's own 1955 ranking
old.hook: Long before today's appellation rules, a 1955 ministerial decree classified a handful of Provence estates; of the original list, eighteen still carry the words 'Cru Classé' on the label, and Domaine de la Croix — founded 1882, left derelict, then bought and wholly replanted after 2001 — is one of them. On the schist and clay above the bay it makes a rosé with more grip and density than the crowd. The pedigree is real, but it was awarded on seniority, not a tasting — a fact worth knowing before you pay for it.

old.name: Seaside sand-terroir Rosé with Tibouren
old.hook: Tibouren is the peninsula's old grape — savoury, faintly orange-tinged, scented with garrigue rather than fruit-candy, and long tied to this stretch of the Saint-Tropez coast. On the sandy, wind-scoured strips between Cap Lardier and Cap Taillat, where Bastide Blanche's vines run nearly to the cliff, it gives a rosé that smells of hot pine and salt. Both houses are certified organic; taste this against a supermarket Provence and you learn what 'saline' actually means. (Bastide Blanche and La Croix are one estate under two labels — don't chase them as rivals.)

old.name: Côtes de Provence Blanc — Rolle by the water
old.hook: Rolle is simply the local name for Vermentino, and by this coast it turns out a white of citrus pith and sea-spray minerality — the natural partner to the fishermen's morning catch on the quay. It is far rarer than the rosé and rarely leaves the region; if you see it, that is the bottle to carry back to the boat.

old.name: Côtes de Provence Rouge — Mourvèdre for the cool evening
old.hook: Provence is not only pink. Mourvèdre and Syrah on the warmer soils give a dark, herb-and-leather red built for a mistral-cool night off the water. Serve it lightly chilled — around 15°C, not room temperature — which is the single correction most people need to make with southern reds.

old.name: Pastis — the shore aperitif ritual
old.hook: The ritual is fixed: a measure of pastis, then roughly five of cold water poured over ice until the clear spirit clouds — the 'louche' — drunk before lunch in the shade. Henri Bardouin blends more than 65 plants and spices where the industrial anise leans on a handful. Honest caveat: it is distilled inland at Forcalquier, in the Haute-Provence back-country, not on the coast — the seaside owns the ritual, the hills own the bottle.

old.label: La Croix-Valmer (248 rue du 8 mai 1945) — ~12 min from Cavalaire
old.hook: The one to book. A caviste-comptoir where the pours run classic to natural, the boards are homemade charcuterie and cheese, and musicians turn up in the evenings. Ask the counter to steer you toward the living bottles rather than the safe rosé.

old.hook: A rare Saint-Tropez address with a conscience: Marylou Contreras cooks generous, seasonal, mostly-organic plates and pours a wine list that runs classic, organic and natural side by side. Warm, small, un-showy in a town that rarely is.

old.name: Fondugues-Pradugues
old.label: Ramatuelle (in the vines
old.hook: A biodynamic estate where you taste the wines by the glass under the parasol pines and eat from L'Éphémère, the on-site food truck. Negligible sulphur, hand-harvest, indigenous ferments — the cleanest expression of 'living wine' the gulf offers to a visitor.

old.name: Bar 1904, Château de la Messardière (Airelles)
old.hook: A dappled-terrace lounge by day, low-lit speakeasy by night, inside a turreted château hotel looking over the Bay of Saint-Tropez and its own park. Come for one impeccable drink, not the room rate.
old.text: A dappled-terrace lounge by day, low-lit speakeasy by night, inside a turreted château hotel looking over the Bay of Saint-Tropez and its own park. Come for one impeccable drink, not the room rate. This is, plausibly, one of the very first bars the Côte d'Azur ever had. The château was a 19th-century wedding gift from cognac merchant Gabriel Dupuy d'Angeac to his daughter Louise. In 1904 Madame de La Messardière began serving refreshments to her glamorous Belle Époque guests — opening what the house counts among the Riviera's earliest bars, and the year the bar takes its name from. It became Airelles' palace after a top-to-bottom restoration, reopening in July 2021. The terroir note: Saint-Tropez's aperitif culture is older and grander than the yacht-set cliché suggests. Honesty: palace prices — a sundowner, not a night out. Signal Verified: refreshments first served 1904 (Mme de La Messardière), among the Côte d'Azur's first bars; Airelles grand reopening 1 July 2021 — Airelles official site

old.name: Bar de La Ménado
old.hook: The outdoor cocktail bar of the beachfront 4-star Hôtel La Ménado — a quiet terrace a stone's throw from the water, serving classic and house-signature cocktails alongside evening sharing platters.
old.text: The outdoor cocktail bar of the beachfront 4-star Hôtel La Ménado — a quiet terrace a stone's throw from the water, serving classic and house-signature cocktails alongside evening sharing platters. This is the sunset-drink move, and its virtue is precisely what it is not: no DJ, no live band, no dance floor — just a terrace, a low sun on the water, and a barman's cocktail. In a town whose evening is modest by design, La Ménado is the calm end of the register, the anti-Rhumerie. The honest caveat is the calendar again: the bar opens only from 15 June to 15 September, so it is a high-summer address and nothing more — outside those three months this stretch of beachfront goes dark early. Signal 148 allée de la Plage; cocktail bar open 15 Jun–15 Sep per the hotel site (lamenado.com), 4-star hotel, beach 20 m away

old.name: La Rhumerie
old.hook: A rum-and-cocktail bar on the marina quay — a bamboo-and-timber terrace over the moored boats, rum-based cocktails, apéro sharing boards, a small dance floor, and band or DJ nights that run late.
old.text: A rum-and-cocktail bar on the marina quay — a bamboo-and-timber terrace over the moored boats, rum-based cocktails, apéro sharing boards, a small dance floor, and band or DJ nights that run late. Cavalaire is a marina town, and after dark its energy collects in the narrow gap between the moored boats and the quay — La Rhumerie is where that energy lands. It is the closest thing the town has to a club, and the honest tell is that it is a bar: apéro-boards, rum cocktails, a dance floor the size of a dinghy. What sets it apart here is the calendar — it works a long February-to-November season when most of the town shutters from autumn to Easter, so it is the port's near-constant. For an actual nightclub you leave: 30–40 minutes to Les Caves du Roy at the Byblos in St-Tropez, or the Ramatuelle/Pampelonne beach clubs (Nikki Beach and neighbours). Cavalaire itself does not pretend to that. Signal Nouveau Port, lot 151; open ~10 Feb–10 Nov, daily ~9:00–03:00; confirmed on Golfe de Saint-Tropez Tourisme and Petit Futé, Yelp listing updated Feb 2026

old.name: Marina Viva Plage
old.hook: A private-beach restaurant and cocktail bar on the sand, with signature drinks timed to sunset — and one of the addresses that throws a party on the two nights the town genuinely does.
old.text: A private-beach restaurant and cocktail bar on the sand, with signature drinks timed to sunset — and one of the addresses that throws a party on the two nights the town genuinely does. It earns its place for a specific, honest reason: on the two dates Cavalaire truly comes alive after dark — the Fête de la Musique on 21 June and Bastille Day on 14 July — the action is on the sand at the beach clubs, and Marina Viva is one that hosts it, staying open into the evening for the fireworks over the bay. That is the lesson about this town's nightlife in a sentence: it lives on the beach and on the calendar, not in a fixed club. Its bar otherwise winds down around 19:00, so any other night it is a sunset cocktail with your feet near the water — modest, seasonal, and none the worse for it. Signal Allée des Anthemis; private-beach restaurant + cocktail bar (creations by Thomas), season opens 24 Apr 2026; hosts a Fête de la Musique tapas-and-rosé evening (21 Jun) and a 14-Juillet fireworks evening per the venue site (marinavivaplage.fr)

old.name: Playa Mezcala
old.hook: A feet-in-the-sand beach club near the Saint-Raphaël end of the bay — breakfast and lunch at the water's edge, a cocktail bar running through the day, tacos and pinsas, and, in high summer, dinner under the stars.
old.text: A feet-in-the-sand beach club near the Saint-Raphaël end of the bay — breakfast and lunch at the water's edge, a cocktail bar running through the day, tacos and pinsas, and, in high summer, dinner under the stars. Cavalaire exists as a resort because of one thing: a long, south-facing arc of sand, so the drink-with-a-view here happens on the beach, not on a rooftop — the town has none. Playa Mezcala grafts a Mexican-cantina conceit onto Var sand (the name, the mezcal, the tacos), exactly the borrowed-elsewhere styling you find all along this coast, even as the kitchen actually plays Mediterranean. Teach the register honestly: outside July and August the bar shuts around 19:00, so for most of the season this is apéro-and-sunset, not a late night; even in high summer it winds down at midnight over dinner, not at 2am. Come for the golden hour with your feet in the sand. Signal 822 avenue de Saint-Raphaël; beach club open daily ~8:30–19:00 (sunbeds and bar), dinner service to midnight only in July–August; official site playamezcala.com + Cavalaire tourism listing, active 2026
